latin: Difficultas intelligendi et ex parte ipsius intellectus et ex parte ipsius intelligibilis prouenire potest.
translation: The difficulty of understanding can arise both from the side of the intellect itself and from the side of the intelligible object itself.
translator: original translation, drafted 2026-09-26 by WRITER-swarm-batch7, from Latin at farmer1998:7970

sources.text: Aristotle, Metaphysics 2.1 (993b4-11), in its common medieval Latin version, as quoted by Thomas Aquinas, Summa contra gentiles 3.45
sources.pico_relation: Edelheit cites this Aristotle passage, and Thomas's use of it, as the background to the thesis

doctrine: Edelheit reports that 'Pico in thesis 40 according to Thomas Aquinas simply presents these two options' — that difficulty in understanding may come from the intellect or from the thing understood — without deciding between them, in the course of surveying how Hennon's Paris commentary on Aristotle's De anima and Metaphysics maps onto Pico's various theses (edelheit2022:2987-2988). Discussing the thesis directly, Edelheit cites Aristotle's Metaphysics 993b4-11 as the reference point (edelheit2022:10270) and quotes, from Thomas's Summa contra gentiles 3.45, the Latin of Aristotle's own image for the difficulty: that our intellect stands to the most evident things in nature 'sicut se habet oculus vespertilionis ad lucem solis', as the eye of the bat (vespertilio) stands to the light of the sun (edelheit2022:10276-10278). The same footnote also gives, in the original Greek, Aristotle's own statement of the point at Metaphysics 993b7-9, 'isos de kai tes chalepotetos ouses kata duo tropous, ouk en tois pragmasin all' en hemin to aition autes...' ('perhaps, since the difficulty is of two kinds, its cause is not in the things but in us...', this English rendering being the entry's own, not a quotation from Edelheit or Farmer) (edelheit2022:10311-10312).
context: Edelheit contrasts Pico's even-handed formulation with the Parisian commentary tradition on Aristotle's Metaphysics (via Hennon), which 'concludes that it comes from our intellect' rather than leaving the question open (edelheit2022:2987-2988), and quotes the Latin of a related, anonymous 'Conclusio responsalis' recorded in Bakker's edition of the Paris commentaries: 'difficultas cognoscendi tam substancias materiales quam inmateriales est ex parte intellectus nostri' ('the difficulty of knowing both material and immaterial substances is on the side of our intellect') (edelheit2022:3006-3008).
reception: Edelheit records that 'thesis 40, just like thesis 20, is included among the theses which were criticized by Bernardo Torni', to be discussed 'again and with further detail in Chapter 12' (edelheit2022:10251); the content of Torni's criticism itself is not given in the material consulted.
historiography: Edelheit (2022) reads thesis 40 as juxtaposing, without adjudicating, the two standard scholastic answers to where cognitive difficulty originates (edelheit2022:2987-2988, 10251), against the background of the Parisian commentary tradition that resolves the question in favor of the intellect (edelheit2022:2987-2988).

quotations.text: Et hoc demonstrant verba Aristotelis in II metaphysicae. Dicit enim ibidem quod difficultas intelligendi res illas accidit ex nobis, non ex illis: nam intellectus noster se habet ad manifestissima rerum sicut se habet oculus vespertilionis ad lucem solis.

not_established: The substance of Bernardo Torni's criticism of thesis 40 is not established from the material consulted; Edelheit defers it to a chapter not excerpted in the packet.
Farmer's cross-reference note on 3>40 as Pico's 'commentary on thesis 7.25 from Averroes' has not been independently verified against 3>40's own text in this entry.

A prior draft quoted an English rendering of Aristotle's bat/sun image, attributed as a Farmer's-note translation at farmer1998:11906, plus an aside that the animal is an 'owl' in Pico per a farmer1998 note to thesis 7.25. On verification: farmer1998:11906 is beyond the end of this uploaded copy of Farmer 1998 (17,719 lines total), and no version of this passage (English, Latin, or Greek) appears anywhere in that file. The passage IS genuinely present in this session's uploaded copy of Edelheit 2022, however: as Thomas Aquinas's Latin quotation of Aristotle (Summa contra gentiles 3.45, quoting Metaphysics 2) at edelheit2022:10276-10278, and again as Aristotle's own Greek at edelheit2022:10311-10312 (Metaphysics 993b7-9). The prior draft's English wording is an accurate rendering of this passage but was misattributed to Farmer; corrected to cite Edelheit's Latin/Greek instead, with the English given only as the entry's own translation, not a quotation. Whether Pico's own thesis 7.25 or Farmer's note to it in fact glosses the animal as an 'owl' rather than a 'bat' is not established by the sources consulted (this uploaded copy of Farmer 1998 was not checked at thesis 7.25 for this entry).
